title: Founder's bookshelf
note: The core ideas of four business books, led by a synthesis of the best of all four, paraphrased from reviews and summaries, never quoting the books' text; buying and reading them is the point. Books do not change, so refresh yearly only to add titles.

groups.label: The synthesis: best of all four

concepts.n: Sell first, then build the system
concepts.s: Get paying customers before anything else, then add structure only as fast as growth demands it.

x.b:
• Masterson: launch before it feels ready; stage one is all selling.
  • Drucker: judge work by outside results, never by effort.
  • Hughes Johnson: write down goals and principles as complexity grows; some of it can wait.

• Until one channel sells reliably, spend most of your week on customers.
  • Add a process only when its absence is costing you now.

Trap: Building org charts, values decks and dashboards before the first repeatable sale.
Synthesis: Masterson sets the order (sell, then systematize); Hughes Johnson supplies the system once you get there.

cards.q: What comes before any company structure, across these books?
cards.a: A repeatable, profitable sale.

cards.q: When should you add a process?
cards.a: When its absence is costing you now, not in anticipation.

cards.q: How does Drucker say to judge your work?
cards.a: By contribution to outside results, never by effort or activity.

concepts.n: Concentrate: few goals, kill the rest
concepts.s: Pick very few priorities, say them often, and deliberately stop everything else.

x.b:
• Drucker: first things first, one at a time; set posteriorities (what you stop).
  • Masterson: kill product tests that don't sell, fast.
  • Hughes Johnson: few clear goals, repeated and reviewed publicly on one cadence.

• Keep a stop-doing list beside the to-do list.
  • Each quarter, drop any project you would not start today.
  • Review goals weekly; review strategy on its own calendar.
Trap: Prioritizing by adding. A ranked list with nothing removed only reorders the overload.

cards.q: What are Drucker's posteriorities?
cards.a: Tasks you deliberately stop doing or never start.

cards.q: What matters more than the goal framework, per Hughes Johnson?
cards.a: Few clear goals, communicated again and again.

cards.q: What does Masterson do with a product test that doesn't sell?
cards.a: Kills it quickly.

concepts.n: Hire for strength and character, by rubric
concepts.s: Hire for one standout strength plus humble, hungry and smart, scored the same way by every interviewer.

x.b:
• Drucker: staff for what someone does uncommonly well; no weakness is no qualification.
  • Lencioni: require humble, hungry and smart together; be strictest on humble.
  • Hughes Johnson: keep a pipeline before you need it, write honest job descriptions, use one rubric.

• One rubric: the role's key strength, then humble, hungry, smart.
  • Debrief on all of it right after each interview.
  • Ask about wins (listen for we vs I) and the biggest failure.

Trap: Panic hiring when a seat opens, or letting a strong résumé override a doubt on humility.
Synthesis: Drucker says what to hire for, Lencioni says who fits a team, Hughes Johnson says how to run the process.

cards.q: Which Lencioni virtue should you be strictest on?
cards.a: Humble.

cards.q: Why does Drucker reject the well-rounded candidate with no standout strength?
cards.a: Absence of weakness is no qualification; you staff for what someone does uncommonly well.

cards.q: What does Hughes Johnson say to build before a seat opens?
cards.a: A recruiting pipeline.

concepts.n: Turn repeat decisions into written rules
concepts.s: When a problem recurs, decide it once as a written principle so others can act without you.

x.b:
• Drucker: classify each problem as generic or exceptional; generic ones get a rule. Seek dissent before deciding.
  • Hughes Johnson: write a mission, long-term goals and principles that settle real trade-offs; teams write charters.

• Second time a question reaches you, write the rule.
  • Delete any value or principle that has never decided anything.
Trap: Patching a recurring problem case by case, or writing slogans that decide nothing.

cards.q: What is Drucker's first question about any problem?
cards.a: Generic or exceptional? Generic problems get a rule.

cards.q: What makes a written principle useful, per Hughes Johnson?
cards.a: It settles a real trade-off so people can decide without asking.

cards.q: Why did Drucker want dissent before a decision?
cards.a: Without it, no one has examined the alternatives.

concepts.s: Measure where your time really goes and write down how you work, because both feel different from how they are.

x.b:
• Drucker: log time in real time, cut and delegate, then pool what is left into big blocks.
  • Hughes Johnson: write a working-with-me guide and ask your team what it gets wrong.
  • Lencioni: "smart" means reading people, which starts with reading yourself.

• Log three to four weeks of time as it happens, about twice a year.
  • Protect one long block a day before meetings refill it.
  • Share your guide; ask new hires to write theirs.
Trap: Reconstructing your week from memory. It flatters you.

cards.q: What are Drucker's three time steps?
cards.a: Record, manage (cut and delegate), consolidate into large blocks.

cards.q: What two parts does a working-with-me guide have?
cards.a: How you like to work, and how you handle work emotionally.

cards.q: What does Lencioni mean by "smart"?
cards.a: Interpersonal common sense: reading people and situations.

concepts.s: Masterson's core rule is to get an imperfect product in front of paying customers fast, then refine it from what the market tells you.

x.b:
• Ready: do just enough preparation to act.
  • Fire: launch and sell before the product is polished.
  • Aim: improve from real customer response.
  • Speed is a competitive weapon: a fast company ships new products before rivals can copy them or offer substitutes.
  • The book itself says this is not reckless action; you still get ready first.

• Set a launch date before the product feels finished.
  • Treat the first sales as the test; customer feedback decides the next version.
  • Fix what buyers complain about, ignore what only you care about.

Trap: Reading it as "skip preparation." The rule cuts excess planning, not the minimum readiness to deliver what you sell.
Trap: Applying it where a failed launch is costly or irreversible: regulated products, safety, or reputations you cannot rebuild.
Synthesis: This is the same instinct as the lean-startup minimum viable product, framed for direct-response marketers. It works best where a launch is cheap to run and cheap to undo.

cards.q: What do "fire" and "aim" stand for in Masterson's rule?
cards.a: Fire is launching and selling before the product is polished; aim is refining it from real customer response.

cards.q: Why does Masterson treat speed as a competitive advantage?
cards.a: A fast company ships new products before competitors can copy them or create substitutes.

cards.q: Does ready, fire, aim mean skipping preparation?
cards.a: No. You still get ready; the rule cuts excess planning that delays the first sale.

cards.q: Where is ready, fire, aim a poor fit?
cards.a: Where a failed launch is costly or hard to undo, such as regulated or safety-critical products.

concepts.s: Masterson argues a business passes through four revenue stages, each with a different main problem and a different job for the founder.

x.b:
Summaries name the stages differently; the most common labels are infancy, childhood, adolescence and adulthood (Shortform uses launch, expand, optimize, sustain). Revenue bands, as summaries give them:

  1. About $0 to $1M: get the first profitable sale. Main skill: selling.
  2. About $1M to $10M: innovate. Launch multiple profitable products quickly.
  3. About $10M to $50M: build systems, structure and real middle management.
  4. About $50M to $100M and up: keep growth going as the company matures; summaries disagree on the details here.

• Name your stage from revenue, then ask what its main problem is.
  • Change your own role as you cross a boundary; each stage needs a different kind of leader.
  • Do not install later-stage systems while you still lack a reliable first sale.

Trap: Treating the dollar bands as precise. They are rough markers; summaries disagree on the upper stages.
Synthesis: The bands fit a direct-response or product business with fast cash cycles. A venture-funded software company can burn through stages on investor money with different problems, so use the model as an order of problems and treat the revenue bands loosely.

cards.q: What is the main problem of Masterson's first stage?
cards.a: Getting the first profitable sale; the key skill is selling.

cards.q: What is the main problem of the second stage (roughly $1M to $10M)?
cards.a: Innovation: launching several profitable products quickly.

cards.q: What does the third stage (roughly $10M to $50M) demand?
cards.a: Systems, structure and capable middle management.

cards.q: What must the founder change at each stage boundary?
cards.a: Their own role and leadership style, since each stage needs a different kind of leader.

concepts.s: In the first stage nothing matters more than selling, so Masterson puts most of the founder's attention on acquiring customers and finding the offer that converts.

x.b:
• Selling is the main skill of stage one.
  • Get the first sales, then find and sharpen the selling proposition from what worked.
  • Masterson calls the fix an Optimal Selling Strategy: the right product, at the right price, sold the right way through the right channel. Summaries describe it as built from four questions.
  • One summary reports he wants about 80 percent of a founder's time on customer acquisition at this stage.

• Track your week: what share went to getting customers?
  • Write down which offer, price and channel produced each sale so far.
  • Cut product work that no buyer has asked for.
Trap: Building infrastructure, branding or hiring before one channel reliably produces profitable sales.

cards.q: What is the dominant skill in Masterson's stage one?
cards.a: Selling: acquiring customers profitably.

cards.q: What does Masterson call his stage-one fix?
cards.a: The Optimal Selling Strategy, a combination of product, price, channel and selling approach that works.

cards.q: In what order does he want the selling proposition and the first sales?
cards.a: First sales, then refine the selling proposition from what worked.

cards.q: Roughly what share of a stage-one founder's time goes to customer acquisition, per one summary?
cards.a: About 80 percent.

concepts.n: Stage two: become an idea factory
concepts.s: Past the first million, Masterson says growth comes from launching many profitable products quickly, usually by improving existing ones.

x.b:
• The company must become an "idea factory" that turns out new profitable products.
  • Improve on existing products instead of inventing something wholly new.
  • Keep speed: test ideas fast and accept quick failures.
  • Give each idea a champion who believes in it, has authority, and has the experience to steer it. No champion, postpone the idea.

• Keep a pipeline of product tests, each with one named owner.
  • Kill tests quickly that do not sell.
  • Start hiring the people who will run the systems of the next stage.

Trap: Launching many products with no owner each. Ideas without a champion stall.
Synthesis: Masterson's second and third stages pull against each other: speed and many launches, then systems and control. The founder's hard job is timing the switch.

cards.q: What does Masterson want the stage-two company to become?
cards.a: An idea factory that launches multiple profitable products quickly.

cards.q: New invention or improvement: which does stage two favor?
cards.a: Improvement on existing products.

cards.q: What three things should an idea's champion have?
cards.a: Belief in the idea, authority to execute, and experience to make good calls.

cards.q: What should you do with an idea that has no champion?
cards.a: Postpone it.

concepts.s: Drucker's first practice is to record how your time is actually spent, cut what wastes it, and pool what remains into large uninterrupted blocks.

x.b:
• Effectiveness can be learned, and it starts with time, the scarcest resource.
  • Memory misreports time use; record it as it happens.
  • Knowledge work needs long uninterrupted stretches; scattered minutes produce little.

1. Record: keep a real-time log for three to four weeks, about twice a year.
  2. Manage: drop activities that produce nothing; hand off what someone else could do as well or better; remove time you waste for others.
  3. Consolidate: bunch the discretionary time left into large blocks, and set deadlines for important work based on it.

Trap: Logging once from memory. A reconstructed log flatters you; the method depends on recording in real time.
Trap: Freeing time and letting meetings refill it. Protect the consolidated block first.

cards.q: What are Drucker's three steps for managing time?
cards.a: Record where time goes, manage it by cutting and delegating, and consolidate discretionary time into large blocks.

cards.q: How long and how often should the time log run?
cards.a: About three to four weeks at a stretch, roughly twice a year.

cards.q: Why must the log be kept in real time?
cards.a: Memory misreports how time was actually spent.

cards.q: What delegation question does the time log prompt?
cards.a: Which of these activities could someone else do just as well or better?

concepts.s: Drucker's effective executive asks what they can contribute to the organization's results, and judges their work by outputs outside their own unit.

x.b:
• Drucker defines an executive as any knowledge worker whose decisions materially affect the organization's results, regardless of title.
  • Effectiveness is getting the right things done; efficiency is doing things right.
  • Look up and out: ask what you can contribute that would change the organization's results.
  • Organizations need performance in three areas: direct results, building and reaffirming values, and developing people for tomorrow.

• Write one line: what result outside my team would change if I did my job very well?
  • Check your goals cover all three areas, not only this quarter's numbers.
  • Raise the standard you set for yourself; Drucker says knowledge workers grow to the demands they make on themselves.
Trap: Measuring yourself by effort or activity. Hours and busyness are inputs; Drucker counts only contribution to results.

cards.q: How does Drucker define an "executive"?
cards.a: Any knowledge worker whose decisions materially affect the organization's ability to get results, whatever the title.

cards.q: What are Drucker's three areas of contribution?
cards.a: Direct results, building and reaffirming values, and developing people for the future.

cards.q: Effectiveness vs efficiency in Drucker's terms?
cards.a: Effectiveness is getting the right things done; efficiency is making resources productive, doing things right.

cards.q: According to Drucker, what determines how far knowledge workers grow?
cards.a: The demands they make on themselves.

concepts.s: Drucker says to staff and work around what people do well, accepting the weaknesses that come with real strength.

x.b:
• Make productive the strengths of your colleagues, your boss and yourself.
  • Staff for what a person can do uncommonly well. Absence of weakness is no qualification.
  • Start from what the organization needs done, then match people's strengths to those key activities.
  • Applied upward: help your boss do what they do well, instead of trying to change them.

• For each report, name the one thing they do better than most; is their role built around it?
  • For a hire, ask "what will this person do exceptionally well?" before "what are their gaps?"

Trap: Hiring the well-rounded candidate with no weaknesses and no standout strength.
Trap: Using strengths as an excuse to ignore a weakness that blocks the job itself, such as integrity.

cards.q: Whose strengths does Drucker say an executive should make productive?
cards.a: Associates', the boss's, and one's own.

cards.q: What should you staff for, in Drucker's view?
cards.a: What a person can do uncommonly well.

cards.q: How does Drucker apply strengths to managing your boss?
cards.a: Help the boss do what they do well rather than trying to change them.

concepts.s: Drucker calls concentration the secret of effectiveness: do the most important things first, one at a time, and deliberately decide what not to do.

x.b:
• Do first things first and one thing at a time.
  • Set "posteriorities": tasks you stop doing or never start. This is the harder half of prioritizing.
  • Drucker treats setting priorities as a test of character more than of analysis.

• Keep a stop-doing list next to your to-do list; add one item weekly.
  • Review old projects regularly and drop those you would not start today.

Trap: Prioritizing by adding. A list of priorities with no posteriorities only reorders the overload.
Synthesis: Drucker's posteriorities match Masterson's advice to kill weak product tests and Hughes Johnson's insistence on few, clear goals. All three books treat saying no as the scarce skill.

cards.q: What does Drucker call the one "secret" of effectiveness?
cards.a: Concentration: first things first, one thing at a time.

cards.q: What are posteriorities?
cards.a: Tasks you decide to stop doing or never start.

cards.q: Why does Drucker call priority-setting a matter of character?
cards.a: The analysis is easy; the hard part is having the courage to drop things.

concepts.s: Drucker's decision process classifies the problem, defines the conditions a solution must meet, decides what is right before compromising, builds in action, and checks results.

x.b:
1. Classify: generic or exceptional? Generic problems get a rule or principle; true exceptions are handled one at a time.
  2. Boundary conditions: state the minimum the decision must achieve.
  3. What is right: work out the right answer before asking what is acceptable; otherwise you cannot tell a good compromise from a bad one.
  4. Build in action: who must know, who must act, with what resources.
  5. Feedback: test the decision against what actually happens.
• Seek dissent. Drucker distrusted decisions reached with no disagreement, because they mean no one examined the alternatives.

Trap: Treating a recurring problem as a one-off. Each patch costs time and the problem keeps coming back; write the rule instead.
Trap: Compromising first. Starting from what is acceptable loses sight of what the decision is for.

cards.q: What is Drucker's first question about any problem?
cards.a: Is it generic or exceptional? Generic problems need a rule; exceptions are handled as they come.

cards.q: What are boundary conditions?
cards.a: The minimum specifications a decision must satisfy to achieve its purpose.

cards.q: Why decide what is right before what is acceptable?
cards.a: Without knowing the right answer you cannot tell a good compromise from a bad one.

cards.q: How did Drucker view a decision reached with no disagreement?
cards.a: With suspicion: no dissent means the alternatives were not examined.

cards.q: What closes Drucker's decision process?
cards.a: Feedback that tests the decision against actual results.

concepts.s: Lencioni's ideal team player has three virtues together: humility, hunger for the team's success, and common sense about people.

x.b:
• Humble: lacks excess ego, shares credit, puts the team first. Lencioni calls it the most important of the three.
  • Hungry: self-motivated, works hard, does what is needed for the team to succeed.
  • Smart: interpersonal common sense, reading people and situations. It has nothing to do with intellect.

Published in 2016, the model grew out of Lencioni's consulting firm, The Table Group.

• The value is in the combination; two out of three produces predictable problems (see the archetypes).
  • A person who cannot be humble is a liability to the team, not only a weak team player.

Trap: Reading "smart" as IQ or technical skill. Lencioni means people sense.
Synthesis: The model screens for behavior on a team. It says nothing about ability to do the job, so use it beside a skills assessment, never instead of one.

cards.q: What are Lencioni's three virtues?
cards.a: Humble, hungry and smart.

cards.q: Which virtue does Lencioni call most important?
cards.a: Humility.

cards.q: What does "smart" mean in this model?
cards.a: Interpersonal common sense: reading people and situations well. It does not mean intellect.

cards.q: What does "hungry" mean?
cards.a: Self-motivated drive to work hard and do whatever helps the team succeed.

concepts.s: Lencioni names the profiles of people who have only one or two of the three virtues, so a manager can spot what is missing.

x.b:
• Accidental mess-maker: humble and hungry, not smart. Means well, creates interpersonal damage without noticing.
  • Lovable slacker: humble and smart, not hungry. Pleasant, does the minimum.
  • Skillful politician: hungry and smart, not humble. Ambitious for self and good at appearing humble; Lencioni treats this as the most dangerous profile.

• Pawn: only humble.
  • Bulldozer: only hungry.
  • Charmer: only smart.
Trap: Using the labels on people casually. Lencioni warns that identifying the profiles accurately is hard and mislabeling a colleague does real damage.

cards.q: Humble and hungry but not smart?
cards.a: The accidental mess-maker.

cards.q: Humble and smart but not hungry?
cards.a: The lovable slacker.

cards.q: Hungry and smart but not humble?
cards.a: The skillful politician, the most dangerous because they can fake humility.

cards.q: Who has only one virtue: humble, hungry, smart?
cards.a: Pawn, bulldozer and charmer respectively.

concepts.s: Lencioni's hiring method turns the three virtues into explicit interview criteria and team debriefs, ahead of technical skills alone.

x.b:
• Hire for the three virtues explicitly; Lencioni urges leaders to stop focusing on technical skills alone.
  • Humility is the virtue to be strictest on.

• Make interviewing a team effort; debrief right after each interview on all three virtues.
  • Use later interviews to probe any lingering doubt. Managers often regret ignoring a red flag.
  • Ask about accomplishments and listen for "we" more than "I"; ask about a biggest failure and ask for specifics.
  • Check references against the three virtues.
  • Tell candidates you hire only humble, hungry, smart people; some self-select out.

Trap: Letting a strong résumé override a doubt on humility. The skillful politician interviews well.
Synthesis: Unstructured interviews are weak predictors in hiring research generally. The model works better as a fixed rubric with the same questions per virtue than as a gut-feel filter, which matches Hughes Johnson's call for a consistent rubric.

cards.q: How does Lencioni structure interview debriefs?
cards.a: Right after each interview, discuss whether the candidate showed humble, hungry and smart.

cards.q: What should you listen for when a candidate describes accomplishments?
cards.a: Whether they say "we" more than "I".

cards.q: Why tell candidates you hire for the three virtues?
cards.a: Some who lack them self-select out.

cards.q: Which archetype is hardest to catch in interviews?
cards.a: The skillful politician, who can appear humble.

concepts.n: Using the model on your current team
concepts.s: Beyond hiring, Lencioni applies the model to assess current employees, develop missing virtues, and embed the virtues in the culture.

x.b:
1. Hiring.
  2. Assessing current employees.
  3. Developing employees weak in a virtue.
  4. Embedding the model in the culture.

The book closes by connecting the model to his earlier Five Dysfunctions of a Team framework. The Table Group also sells an assessment built on the model.

• Have each team member rate themselves on the three virtues, then discuss in one-to-ones.
  • Coach one virtue at a time with specific, observed behavior.
  • Use the same vocabulary in reviews, recognition and hiring so the culture stays consistent.
Trap: Using the model as a ranking or firing tool. Its main value is a shared language for coaching; labeling people publicly backfires.

cards.q: What are Lencioni's four applications of the model?
cards.a: Hiring, assessing current employees, developing employees, and embedding the model in the culture.

cards.q: Which earlier Lencioni framework does the book connect to?
cards.a: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.

cards.q: What is the safer main use of the model on a current team?
cards.a: A shared language for coaching specific behaviors.

concepts.n: Founding documents and the operating system
concepts.s: Hughes Johnson argues a growing company should write down why it exists, where it is going and how it decides, then run on a regular planning and review rhythm.

x.b:
• Founding documents: mission, long-term goals, and principles or values. Teams write a smaller charter of their own.
  • Operating system: make recurring ways of setting goals, reviewing work and deciding explicit as complexity grows.
  • Some of this can wait until the company has traction and knows what it is.

• Write the mission and a few long-term goals in plain language; revisit yearly.
  • Write principles that settle real trade-offs, so people can decide without asking you.
  • Ask each team for a charter: purpose, goals, how it works with other teams.

Trap: Writing values as slogans that settle no trade-off. If a principle never decides anything, delete it.
Synthesis: This is Drucker's generic-decision rule applied to the whole company: principles turn recurring choices into rules so leaders spend their time on the exceptions.

cards.q: What are the core founding documents in Scaling People?
cards.a: Mission, long-term goals, and principles or values; teams add their own charter.

cards.q: What does Hughes Johnson mean by an operating system?
cards.a: The explicit, recurring way a company sets goals, reviews work and makes decisions.

cards.q: When can founding documents wait?
cards.a: Until the company has traction and knows what it is.

concepts.s: Hughes Johnson favors few clear goals, repeated often and reviewed publicly on one predictable cadence, with separate metrics and strategy reviews.

x.b:
• The goal framework matters less than clear goals communicated again and again.
  • Review the company's top goals and metrics publicly, with everyone.
  • Keep one predictable cadence for planning and review.
  • Track input (leading) metrics alongside output metrics; at Stripe, managers tracked input, operational and strategic metrics.

• Meet your team weekly to review progress.
  • Put metrics reviews and strategy reviews on separate calendars so each happens.
  • For each output goal, name the input metric your team actually controls.
Trap: Frequent metrics reviews with rare strategy reviews. The metrics review quietly becomes the strategy review, and strategy shrinks to this week's numbers.

cards.q: What matters more than the choice of goal framework, per Hughes Johnson?
cards.a: Clear goals and repeated communication of them.

cards.q: What goes wrong when metrics reviews are frequent and strategy reviews rare?
cards.a: The metrics review becomes the strategy review.

cards.q: Why track input metrics?
cards.a: They are leading indicators that teams control, unlike lagging output metrics.

cards.q: How often does she suggest reviewing progress with your team?
cards.a: Weekly.

concepts.s: Hughes Johnson treats hiring as a built process: a steady pipeline, honest job descriptions, and the same rubric used by every interviewer.

x.b:
• Hiring quality comes from process: pipeline, honest description, consistent scoring.
  • Her background: about ten years at Google, then Stripe COO from 2014 to 2021, scaling it from under 200 people to several thousand.

• Build a recruiting pipeline before you need to fill a role.
  • Write job descriptions that state the real work; she warns against ones that only sell a warm picture of the company.
  • Use one simple rubric for every interviewer and candidate.

Trap: Hiring in a panic when a seat opens. Without a pipeline you lower the bar to fill the gap.
Synthesis: Hughes Johnson supplies the process and Lencioni supplies the behavioral criteria. A rubric that scores both job skills and humble, hungry, smart combines them.

cards.q: What does Hughes Johnson say is the first step to hiring well?
cards.a: Building a recruiting pipeline.

cards.q: What job-description mistake does she warn against?
cards.a: Selling a warm picture of the company instead of stating the real work.

cards.q: What keeps interviews comparable across candidates?
cards.a: A simple, consistent assessment rubric used throughout.

concepts.s: Hughes Johnson starts management with self-awareness, made concrete in a written working-with-me guide, and asks for direct, observed feedback in both directions.

x.b:
• Effective leadership starts with self-awareness.
  • Write a working with me guide with two parts: how you like to work, and how you handle work emotionally.
  • Share it and ask for feedback on it; the exchange becomes a mutual feedback session.
  • Say the thing you think you cannot say; beware over-filtering.
  • Observe someone's performance across several situations before giving feedback.

• Draft your guide in 30 minutes, give it to your team, and ask what is missing.
  • Ask new hires to write one in their first weeks.
  • Before a hard conversation, list two or three observed examples.

Trap: Treating the guide as a rulebook others must adapt to. It is a starting point for mutual adjustment.
Synthesis: Drucker's build-on-strengths and Lencioni's "smart" virtue both depend on the self-knowledge this guide forces. Of the four books, Hughes Johnson gives the most concrete tool for getting it.

cards.q: What two parts should a working-with-me guide have?
cards.a: How you like to work, and how you handle work emotionally.

cards.q: What should you do after writing your guide?
cards.a: Share it and ask for feedback, turning it into a mutual feedback session.

cards.q: What should precede giving someone feedback?
cards.a: Observing their performance across several situations.

cards.q: What does "say the thing you think you cannot say" guard against?
cards.a: Over-filtering important feedback.
